The physics: what molecular dynamics does¶

Molecular dynamics answers a simple question with a lot of consequences: if we knew the force on every atom, and we integrated Newton's equations of motion for all of them, what would the material do?

The machinery is exactly what you built in A1. Positions and velocities evolve under

mid2𝐫idt2=𝐅i=−∇iU(𝐫1,…,𝐫N),

integrated with velocity-Verlet. What changes is the potential energy U, and the consequences of that change reach into every part of the program:

  • The interactions are short ranged. Gravity reaches across the solar system, so A1 could afford all N(N−1)/2 pairs. The Lennard-Jones interaction is negligible beyond a few molecular diameters, so we cut it off and only ever look at nearby pairs. That is what the cell-linked list and Verlet neighbour list in the provided code are for: they turn an O(N2) force evaluation into O(N).
  • The system is periodic. A few thousand molecules in a box with walls would be almost all surface. Periodic boundary conditions with the minimum-image convention give a bulk liquid instead.
  • The molecules have internal structure. Besides the non-bonded interactions there are bonds, angles and torsions, which is where the chemistry of pentane enters.
  • Temperature is a thing you control. A thermostat lets you sample a constant-temperature (NVT) ensemble instead of constant energy (NVE).

Why any of this is worth doing: from the trajectory you can measure quantities that are hard or impossible to get any other way. In this assignment you measure two of them, each testing a different layer of the simulation. The conformer populations test the free-energy landscape of a single molecule, and reveal the pentane effect, a genuinely subtle piece of chemistry. The mean-squared displacement gives a transport coefficient, the self-diffusion coefficient, through the Einstein relation

⟨|𝐫cm(t)−𝐫cm(0)|2⟩→ t large 6Dt.

The model: a united-atom force field for n-pentane¶

The molecule. n-Pentane is CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3. We do not simulate the hydrogens. In a united-atom model each CH3 or CH2 group is one interaction site with the mass of the whole group. Two reasons: it removes two thirds of the sites, and, more importantly, it removes the fastest motion in the system. A C-H bond vibrates with a period of about 10 fs, which would force a time step of roughly 0.1 fs; without hydrogens, 1 fs is enough.

Each molecule therefore has 5 sites, 4 bonds, 3 angles and 2 dihedrals (ϕ1 over atoms 1-2-3-4 and ϕ2 over atoms 2-3-4-5). The two dihedrals share three atoms, which is what makes their statistics coupled rather than independent, and that coupling is the subject of task C2.

State point: density ρ=626 kg/m3 and T=293 K, which is liquid pentane at ambient conditions.

Non-bonded: Lennard-Jones¶

ULJ(r)=4ϵ[(σr)12−(σr)6]−ULJ(rcut)for r≤rcut,

and zero beyond. Use rcut=14 Å. The r−6 term is the attractive dispersion interaction that holds the liquid together; the r−12 term is the repulsion that keeps sites apart. Subtracting ULJ(rcut) shifts the potential to zero at the cut-off, so that no energy jump occurs when a pair crosses it.

Site ϵ/kB (K) σ (Å) mass (amu)
CH3 98.0 3.75 15.035
CH2 46.0 3.95 14.027

Cross terms follow the Lorentz-Berthelot mixing rules, σij=12(σi+σj) and ϵij=ϵiiϵjj.

Exclusions. Within a molecule, the 1-2, 1-3 and 1-4 pairs must not interact through Lennard-Jones: their geometry is already fixed by the bond, angle and torsion terms, and counting both would be double counting. The 1-5 pair does interact, and that single interaction, between the two end groups, is what makes the pentane effect of task C2 appear.

Bonded terms¶

Ubond(r)=12kb(r−r0)2,r0=1.54 Å,kb/kB=3.19×105 K/Å2,

Uangle(θ)=12kθ(θ−θ0)2,θ0=114∘,kθ/kB=6.25×104 K rad−2.

For each of the two dihedral angles, the Ryckaert-Bellemans torsion

Utors(ϕ)=c0+c1cosϕ+c2cos2ϕ+c3cos3ϕ,

c0/kB=1010.0 K,c1/kB=−2018.9 K,c2/kB=136.4 K,c3/kB=3165.3 K.

This has its global minimum at ϕ=180∘ (trans) and local minima near ±60∘ (gauche), separated by barriers of several kBT. Those barriers are the reason conformer statistics converge slowly: a molecule sits in one state for a long time and flips rarely, so what you are sampling is a rare event, which task C2 asks you to think about quantitatively.

A force field like this one is empirical: the functional forms are chosen for convenience and the parameters are fitted, here to thermodynamic data for alkanes. Nothing guarantees it reproduces a property it was not fitted to. That is the difference between verification (Part B: does my code implement this model correctly?) and validation (Part C: does this model describe real pentane?).

The code, and your working environment¶

The starting code is MD_student_v7.0.0.zip under Files ▸ Code. It is a working Lennard-Jones molecular dynamics program: your job is to extend it into a pentane simulator. Unpacking it gives you a folder MD_student_v7.0.0; rename that to code/ in your working directory, so that the paths in this notebook and in the hand-in layout line up.

Then: constants.h (compile-time constants), structs.h (all data types), memory.c (allocation and freeing), setparameters.c (the only place run configuration lives: there are no input files, you recompile to change a run), random.c, initialise.c (initial positions, velocities, topology), nbrlist.c (cell-linked list and Verlet neighbour list), forces.c (your main work site), dynamics.c (the velocity-Verlet halves, boundary conditions, thermostat), fileoutput.c (.pdb trajectories and restart files), and force_test.c (the finite-difference force and virial checker you will use in B3 and B5).

gcc -O3 *.c -o md -lm                      # production
gcc -g -Wall -Wextra *.c -o md_debug -lm   # debugging
./md > run.csv

House rules when extending. New functions get a prototype in the matching .h. New per-particle arrays are added to a struct in structs.h, allocated in alloc_memory and freed in free_memory. Internal units are the reduced units of task A1, not SI.

# Shared imports, constants and two small helper functions for the analysis cells below.
import re
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

PS_PER_TIME_UNIT = 1.0967   # one internal time unit in ps (t0 from A1)
T_TARGET = 293.0            # target temperature in K
FD_TOL = 5e-5               # accepted relative tolerance of the finite-difference test (B3)


def load_csv(path):
    """Read a CSV file. Files redirected from PowerShell are UTF-16."""
    try:
        return pd.read_csv(path)
    except UnicodeError:
        return pd.read_csv(path, encoding="utf-16")


def energy_drift(time, etot):
    """Fit Etot = slope * time + intercept.

    slope           -> systematic drift
    residual        -> what is left after removing the line (the bounded oscillation)
    rel_oscillation -> half peak-to-peak of the residual, divided by |mean Etot|
    """
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(time, etot, 1)
    mean = np.mean(etot)
    residual = etot - (slope * time + intercept)
    half_range = 0.5 * (residual.max() - residual.min())
    return {
        "mean": mean,
        "slope": slope,
        "rel_drift": slope / abs(mean),
        "residual": residual,
        "rel_oscillation": half_range / abs(mean),
    }

Part A: Modeling¶

In the oral you should be able to: state your unit system and convert any quantity in this notebook to SI; derive each bonded force from its potential; explain why the four torsion forces sum to zero and exert no net torque.

A1) Units¶

It is common practice to introduce non-standard units in simulations. In your code, use Kelvin for the energy scale (that is, the energy unit is kB×1 K), Å for distances, and atomic mass units (amu) for masses. The time unit follows from these.

Deliver: the derivation of the time unit, its value in SI, and the time step of 1 fs expressed in internal units. State also the internal-unit values you will use for ϵ, σ, kb and kθ, and one sanity check that your conversion is right (for example, the thermal velocity of a CH2 site at 293 K, in both unit systems).

Answer A1: Units¶

Base units¶

  • We choose energy, length and mass as the base units. Every other unit follows from them.
  • A quantity in internal units is its SI value divided by the unit. A star (*) marks an internal value.
Quantity Unit SI value
Energy E0 = kB × 1 K 1.380649×10-23 J
Length L0 = 1 Å 10-10 m
Mass M0 = 1 amu 1.66054×10-27 kg

Time unit¶

  • Energy has dimensions mass × length² / time², so the three units must satisfy

E0=M0L02t02.

  • Solving for the time unit:

t0=M0L02E0=(1.66054×10−27)(10−10)21.380649×10−23≈1.0967×10−12 s=1.0967 ps.

  • Why? Once energy, length and mass are fixed, time is no longer free. It is the only unit that makes E=ML2/t2 hold.
  • The 1 fs time step in internal units is

Δt*=10−15 s1.0967×10−12 s≈9.1184×10−4.

  • Handy conversion: 1 ps=0.9118 internal time units.

Force-field parameters in internal units¶

  • ϵ/kB is given in kelvin and σ in Å. These are already our base units, so the numbers carry over unchanged.
Site type ε* σ* m*
CH3 98.0 3.75 15.035
CH2 46.0 3.95 14.027
  • For a mixed CH3-CH2 pair, Lorentz-Berthelot gives

ϵ32*=98.0×46.0≈67.1416,σ32*=3.75+3.952=3.85.

Parameter Internal value Reason
kb* 3.19×105 energy / length², so kb L02 / E0 is just the number in K/Å²
r0* 1.54 length in Å
kθ* 6.25×104 energy per rad²; the angle must be in radians
θ0 1.98968 rad 114° × π/180
rcut* 14 length in Å

Sanity check: thermal speed of a CH2 site at 293 K¶

  • We use the 3D root-mean-square speed.

vrms=3kBTm.

  • Route 1, in SI. The site mass is m=14.027×1.66054×10−27=2.32924×10−26 kg, so

vrms=3(1.380649×10−23)(293)2.32924×10−26≈721.8 m/s.

  • Route 2, in internal units. Here kBT/E0=293 and m*=14.027, so

vrms*=3(293)14.027≈7.9161.

  • The velocity unit is v0=L0/t0=10−10/1.0967×10−12≈91.184 m/s. Converting back:

7.9161×91.184≈721.8 m/s.

  • Conclusion: both routes give 721.8 m/s, so our conversion is consistent.

A2) Bonded forces¶

From the expressions for the bond, angle, and torsion potentials, derive the corresponding forces. Express them in terms of the bond vectors 𝐫ij, 𝐫kj, and 𝐫kl as defined in forces.c.

Deliver, for each of the three terms: the force on every participating atom, and one sentence on how the expression behaves in an obvious limit (for instance at the potential minimum). State explicitly why the four torsion forces sum to zero and carry no net torque, and describe the numerical test that would confirm both properties on your own implementation.

Answer A2: Bonded forces¶

Starting point¶

  • The force on an atom is minus the gradient of the energy, so it points towards lower energy.

Fs=−∇rsU

  • Method for all three terms: write U as a function of one scalar (bond length, angle, or cosϕ). Then use the chain rule to get from that scalar to the atom positions.
  • In forces.c the bond vectors are the following. The minimum-image convention is already applied to them.
Vector Definition Points from
rij ri - rj j to i
rkj rk - rj j to k
rkl rk - rl l to k
  • The forces below belong to one interaction. In the code they are added to the total force on each atom.

1. Bond stretch (atoms i and j)¶

Setup. Let a=rij and r=|a|. The energy is

Ub=12kb(r−r0)2.

It penalises both stretching and compression.

Slope of the energy with respect to the length:

dUbdr=kb(r−r0).

Slope of the length with respect to the position of atom i:

∇rir=ar.

  • Why? Moving atom i away from j by a small step ds changes the length by dr=(a/r)·ds. Only the component of the step along the bond matters, so the gradient is the unit vector along the bond.

Chain rule:

Fi=−kb(r−r0)ar,Fj=−Fi.

  • Why Fj=−Fi? The energy only depends on ri−rj. Moving j by ds has exactly the opposite effect of moving i by ds.
  • Limit check: at r=r0 both forces are zero. A stretched bond pulls the atoms together, and a compressed bond pushes them apart.

2. Angle bend (atoms i, j, k, with j in the middle)¶

Setup. Let a=rij, b=rkj, a=|a|, b=|b|. The angle comes from the dot product:

q=cosθ=a·bab,Uθ=12kθ(θ−θ0)2.

Chain of dependence. Positions change the bond vectors. The bond vectors change q, then θ, then U. So

Fi=−dUθdθdθdq∇riq.

  • Why go through q? A dot product is easy to differentiate with respect to vectors. θ itself is not.

The two scalar derivatives:

dUθdθ=kθ(θ−θ0),dθdq=−1sinθ.

  • Why? θ=arccosq, and the derivative of arccosq is −1/1−q2=−1/sinθ.

Gradient of q. Moving atom i changes only a. Moving atom k changes only b. The product rule on q=(a·b)/(ab) gives

∇riq=bab−qaa2,∇rkq=aab−qbb2.

  • Why two terms? q depends on a in the numerator (a·b) and in the denominator (a=|a|). The first term is the numerator part. The second term is the denominator part, using ∇aa=a/a.

Combine. The minus sign of the force cancels the minus sign of dθ/dq:

Fi=kθ(θ−θ0)sinθ(bab−cosθaa2)

Fk=kθ(θ−θ0)sinθ(aab−cosθbb2)

Central atom. Moving j changes both vectors, each with a minus sign (a=ri−rj and b=rk−rj). The result is

Fj=−Fi−Fk.

  • Why? Moving all three atoms together changes no angle. So the three forces must add up to zero.

Intuition: the bracket in Fi is the part of b/(ab) that is perpendicular to a. So the force on atom i is perpendicular to its own bond. It swings atom i around the central atom and never stretches the bond. The bond-length force is a separate term.

Limit checks

  • At θ=θ0 all three forces are zero.
  • Fi·a=0, because a·bab−cosθ=0. The force is purely a bending force.
  • The formulas need nonzero bond lengths and 0<θ<π, and the angle must be in radians.

3. Torsion (atoms i, j, k, l)¶

3a. Geometry¶
  • Bond vectors: a=rij, b=rkj, c=rkl.
  • Each plane (atoms ijk and jkl) has a normal vector, from a cross product:

n=a×b,m=b×c,N=|n|,M=|m|.

  • The torsion angle is the angle between the two planes, which is the angle between their normals:

q=cosϕ=n·mNM.

  • With these definitions, trans gives opposite normals. So q=−1 and ϕ=π, as the assignment requires.
  • Why cosϕ and not ϕ? The torsion energy is a polynomial in cosϕ. We never need ϕ itself, so there is no arccos, no sign ambiguity and no singularity at 0 or π.
3b. Slope of the energy¶
  • The energy depends on ϕ only through q:

Uϕ=c0+c1q+c2q2+c3q3.

  • Define its slope with respect to q:

H=dUϕdq=c1+2c2q+3c3q2.

  • Then for every atom s the chain rule gives

Fs=−H∇rsq.

  • What remains is the gradient of q with respect to the atom positions.
3c. Gradient of q with respect to the two normals¶
  • q is a normalised dot product of n and m. This is the same form as cosθ in the angle case, so the same product rule applies:

A=∇nq=mNM−qnN2,B=∇mq=nNM−qmM2.

  • A and B are only intermediate quantities. They are not forces.
3d. From the normals to the bond vectors¶

Step 1: the total change of q. q depends on two vectors, n and m. For a small change of the atoms, each vector changes a little, and each change moves q by "gradient times change". The two contributions add:

dq=A·dn+B·dm.

Intuition: this is the multivariable chain rule. If a quantity depends on two inputs, its total change is the change caused by the first input plus the change caused by the second. The vectors A and B are exactly the "sensitivities" of q to n and to m.

Step 2: how the normals change. n=a×b depends on two vectors, so the product rule applies to each factor in turn. The same holds for m:

dn=da×b+a×db,dm=db×c+b×dc.

Step 3: insert into dq.

dq=A·(da×b)+A·(a×db)+B·(db×c)+B·(b×dc).

Step 4: isolate each da, db, dc. A scalar triple product is unchanged when its three vectors are rotated cyclically: X·(Y×Z)=Y·(Z×X). We use it to move every small change to the front:

Term After the cyclic swap
A·(da × b) da · (b × A)
A·(a × db) db · (A × a)
B·(db × c) db · (c × B)
B·(b × dc) dc · (B × b)

Step 5: collect. Now dq has the form ga·da+gb·db+gc·dc, with

ga=b×A,gb=A×a+c×B,gc=B×b.

  • ga, gb, gc are the gradients of q with respect to a, b and c. The dot product form shows this, because "change in q = gradient · change in the vector".
3e. From bond-vector gradients to atom gradients¶
  • Each atom position enters only through the bond vectors that contain it:

a=ri−rj,b=rk−rj,c=rk−rl.

  • If an atom is the first point of a vector, moving the atom changes that vector by +dr. If it is the second point, the change is −dr.
  • If the atom appears in several vectors, we add up the contributions.
Atom moved Bond vectors it appears in Gradient of q
i a (+) ga
j a (-), b (-) -ga - gb
k b (+), c (+) gb + gc
l c (-) -gc

Intuition: think of it as bookkeeping. To find how q responds to moving atom k, list every bond vector that contains rk (here b and c). Each one passes its own sensitivity on, with a plus sign when k is the tip of the vector and a minus sign when k is the tail. Atom j sits at the tail of both a and b, so both signs are negative.

3f. The four torsion forces¶
  • Multiply each gradient by −H:

Fi=−Hga,Fj=H(ga+gb),

Fk=−H(gb+gc),Fl=Hgc.

3g. Limit checks¶
  • At trans the unit normals are opposite, so A=B=0 and all four forces vanish.
  • At an interior gauche minimum H=0, so the forces vanish as well.
  • The formulas need N≠0 and M≠0. A collinear triplet does not define a plane.

4. Why the four torsion forces sum to zero and give no net torque¶

Net force¶
  • Add the four results. All terms cancel in pairs:

∑sFs=−Hga+H(ga+gb)−H(gb+gc)+Hgc=0.

  • Why? Moving all four atoms by the same vector changes no bond vector, so ϕ and U stay the same. Translation cannot change the energy, so the forces cannot add up to a net push.

Intuition: the torsion is an internal interaction of the four atoms. It can push atoms against each other, but it cannot push the group as a whole. Its centre of mass feels no force from it.

Net torque¶
  • Rotate the whole four-atom group rigidly by a small angle. The vector δω points along the rotation axis, and its length is the angle. Every atom moves by

δrs=δω×(rs−R),

where R is a point on the axis.

  • A rigid rotation changes no bond length or angle, so ϕ and U stay the same. To first order, the energy change is minus the work done by the forces:

δU=−∑sFs·δrs=−δω·∑s(rs−R)×Fs.

  • The second form uses the cyclic swap of the triple product again.
  • δU=0 holds for every direction of δω. So the vector it is multiplied with must be zero:

∑s(rs−R)×Fs=0.

What does this sum mean physically?

  • The vector (rs−R)×Fs is the torque of force Fs about R. It measures how strongly that force tries to spin the group about R.
  • The total torque is the sum over the four atoms. Zero means the four forces try to spin the group in opposite ways that exactly cancel.
  • Why the origin does not matter: changing R changes the sum by −ΔR×∑sFs, which is zero because the net force is zero.

Intuition: the torsion can twist one end of the molecule relative to the other. That changes the shape but it cannot make the molecule spin faster as a whole. So it conserves the total angular momentum, just as the zero net force conserves the total momentum. The same idea also explains why the interaction only depends on the internal angle ϕ and not on where or how the four atoms sit in space.

5. Numerical tests of our implementation¶

Test configuration

  • We use a noncollinear geometry from a thermalised single molecule.
  • We do not use the freshly built chain. There all bonded forces are zero, so the test would compare round-off with round-off.

Test 1: net force and net torque of each torsion

Fnet=∑sFs,τnet=∑s(rs−R)×Fs.

  • The torque needs positions that are not wrapped by the periodic box. Taking atom j as the origin:
Atom Position
j xj = 0
i xi = a
k xk = b
l xl = b - c
  • Both results must be zero up to round-off.
  • We also report them relative to the size of the individual forces:

ηF=|Fnet|∑s|Fs|,ητ=|τnet|∑s|xs||Fs|.

Test 2: finite differences, for each bonded term separately

  • We displace one atom by a small distance δ along one axis, with all other coordinates fixed:

FsαFD=−U(rs+δeα)−U(rs−δeα)2δ.

What each test proves

Test What it proves
Net force and torque the torsion is invariant under translation and rotation
Finite differences the coded forces equal the negative gradient of the coded energy

Part B: Implementation and testing¶

In the oral you should be able to: walk through any force routine you wrote and justify it line by line; explain what the finite-difference force test proves and what it cannot catch; explain why the test must run from an equilibrated configuration; explain why energy conservation is tested in NVE and how the drift should scale with the timestep.

Throughout Part B, every claim of correctness needs a number: a relative error, a drift, a tolerance. "It looks fine" is not a verification.

B1) I/O¶

Output diagnostic data (the energies and the temperature) to CSV every few steps, either by redirecting stdout or by writing a file. Every plot in this notebook loads from data/.

Answer B1: I/O¶

  • Where: main writes CSV to standard output every num_dt_output steps.
  • When: after both velocity-Verlet half updates, so Epot and Ekin belong to the same full time step.
  • Columns: step, internal time, potential energy, kinetic energy, total energy, temperature.
  • How we saved it: we redirected the output with ./md > ../data/test.csv. The file is test.csv.
  • Units: energy is in kBK, so the number we get for T is directly in kelvin.

Temperature. For N=2000 sites:

T=2Ekin3N−3.

  • Why 3N−3? There are 3N velocity components. The total momentum is fixed at zero, which removes three of them.
  • Why the factor 2? Equipartition gives Ekin=12kBT per degree of freedom.

B2) Particle types and non-bonded forces¶

Implement particle typing (CH3 and CH2) using the type array in Vectors: extend initialise_types. Take the type-dependent masses into account in the velocity updates and in the kinetic energy. Implement the LJ forces with Lorentz-Berthelot parameters selected per pair type.

B3) Test the non-bonded forces¶

Verify correctness with the provided finite-difference checker (force_test.c) from an equilibrated configuration, and demonstrate long-time energy conservation in NVE at the target density.

Deliver:

  • a table of the finite-difference test: the largest relative error over the particles, for the force and for the virial, with the displacement step you used and the tolerance you accepted;
  • a figure of total, kinetic and potential energy against time for an NVE run at the target density;
  • a number: the relative energy drift per unit time, and what it becomes when you halve the time step. State the scaling you expected and whether you observed it. Separate the bounded oscillation of Etot from any systematic slope before you quote a scaling: they need not behave the same way, and only one of them is the integrator's own error.
  • a check on your masses: the temperature implied by each site type separately, from the mean square velocity of its own sites, next to the set point. The two types have different masses but must give the same temperature. Nothing else in this assignment tests that you used the right mass for the right site: the force test never touches masses, and energy is conserved just as happily with the wrong ones. If your two numbers disagree, say whether that is your typing, your time step or your equilibration, and show the run that decides it.

Then explain, in two or three sentences, why running this test from the initial lattice instead of an equilibrated configuration would hide errors.

On the tolerance: do not pick one out of the air. Estimate the accuracy the check itself can reach. It differences two nearly equal potential energies, so it loses digits in proportion to how large that energy is compared with the change a displacement of δ produces, and the resulting floor is absolute, which means it hurts your smallest forces most. Work out roughly where that floor sits for your system and accept a tolerance a little above it.

Answer B2-B3: Types and non-bonded forces¶

B2: Implementation¶

Particle types

  • initialise_types() assigns the repeating pattern CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3 to each molecule.
Site type Mass (amu) ε/kB (K) σ (Å)
CH3 15.035 98.0 3.75
CH2 14.027 46.0 3.95
  • The mass is looked up from the type in the velocity-Verlet velocity update and in the kinetic energy.

Initial velocities

  • Each site gets a Gaussian velocity with a type-dependent width:

v∝kBTmi.

  • Why? Equipartition gives every site the same mean kinetic energy, so heavier sites move more slowly.
  • We remove the centre-of-mass velocity with a mass-weighted average:

vCM=∑imivi∑imi.

  • Why mass-weighted? The total momentum is ∑imivi. With two different masses, subtracting the plain mean velocity would leave a net momentum.

Lennard-Jones for unlike pairs

  • We use the Lorentz-Berthelot rules:

σij=σi+σj2,ϵij=ϵiϵj.

  • The pair values are used in the LJ force and in the potential shift at the cut-off.

B3a: Finite-difference test of the LJ forces¶

  • We ran the supplied force_test.c from an equilibrated configuration.
Quantity Value
Largest particle-force relative error 5.709×10-6
Virial relative error 1.360×10-9
Displacement δ 10-6 Å
Accepted relative tolerance 5×10-5

Where the tolerance comes from

  • The test subtracts two nearly equal energies, so round-off limits it. The absolute noise in the force is

Fnoise≈16ϵmachine|U|δ.

  • Why is the floor absolute? The round-off in U is about ϵmachine|U| whatever the force is. Dividing by δ gives a fixed force error. It hurts the smallest forces most, in relative terms.
Quantity Value
Fnoise (internal force units) 4.336×10-3
Smallest tested force Fmin 1.360×102
Worst relative floor Fnoise/Fmin 3.19×10-5
Accepted tolerance 5×10-5
Observed largest error 5.7×10-6
  • We chose a tolerance just above the floor. The observed error is well below it, so the test passes.

Why not from the initial lattice?

  • A lattice is highly symmetric, so many forces cancel or are tiny.
  • Then the relative error is dominated by round-off and can hide real mistakes.
  • An equilibrated configuration gives generic, non-zero forces.

B3b: NVE energy conservation¶

  • We ran two NVE simulations from the same equilibrated state at 626 kg/m3.
    • The first used 1 fs.
    • The second used 0.5 fs, with twice as many steps, so both cover the same time.
  • The figure below shows the energies. Epot and Ekin exchange energy. Etot stays nearly constant.

Systematic drift

  • We fit a line Etot(t)=at+b and quote

relative drift=a|⟨Etot⟩|.

Time step Relative drift per internal time unit
1 fs -6.381×10-8
0.5 fs -1.045×10-8
  • Both drifts are tiny, so there is no significant systematic gain or loss of energy.
  • The ratio of the two drifts is about 6.1, not 4. We do not expect a clean scaling for the slope, and we do not claim one.

Bounded oscillation

  • We subtract the linear fit first and then take the half peak-to-peak of the rest.
  • Why separate them? The bounded wiggle is the integrator's own error. A slope can come from other sources, so the two need not scale in the same way.
  • Velocity-Verlet is a second-order method, so the bounded error should scale as

ΔE∝(Δt)2.

  • Why (Δt)2? Each step has a local error of order Δt3, which gives a global error of order Δt2. Velocity-Verlet also conserves a slightly modified energy almost exactly, so the error oscillates and does not grow.
  • Halving the step should therefore reduce the error by 22=4.
Quantity Value
Expected ratio (1 fs / 0.5 fs) 4
Measured ratio 3.890
  • The measured ratio is close to 4, as expected for a second-order method.

B3c: Mass check (temperature per site type)¶

  • For each site type α we compute the temperature from the mean square velocity of its own sites:

Tα=∑i∈αmivi23Nα.

  • We used a short NVT continuation from the equilibrated configuration.
Population Mean temperature (K) Target (K)
Whole system 293.009 293
CH3 292.885 293
CH2 292.848 293
  • The difference is TCH3−TCH2=0.037 K.
  • Conclusion: the two types have different masses but give the same temperature, and both match 293 K. So our code uses the right mass for each site.

Likely oral questions¶

  • What does the finite-difference test prove? The coded force equals minus the gradient of the coded energy, and the virial is consistent with it.
  • What can it not catch? A wrong potential: wrong parameters, mixing rule, masses or exclusions. The force and the energy would be wrong in the same way.
  • Why NVE for energy conservation? The thermostat adds or removes energy. Only NVE isolates the error of the integrator.

nve_05fs = load_csv("data/b3_nve_05fs.csv")

print("1 fs columns :", list(nve_1fs.columns))

ax.plot(nve_1fs["time"], nve_1fs["Epot"], label="Potential energy")
ax.plot(nve_1fs["time"], nve_1fs["Ekin"], label="Kinetic energy")

    "Relative bounded oscillation": [result_1fs["rel_oscillation"], result_05fs["rel_oscillation"]],
})
display(energy_table)

# Velocity-Verlet is second order: halving the step should reduce the bounded error by 4
ratio = result_1fs["rel_oscillation"] / result_05fs["rel_oscillation"]
print()

# --- Figure: bounded energy error after removing the drift ---------------

ax.plot(nve_05fs["time"], result_05fs["residual"] / abs(result_05fs["mean"]), label="0.5 fs")

# --- Finite-difference force test: read the output of force_test.c -------
fd_text = Path("data/b3_force_test.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-16")

force_errors = [float(x) for x in re.findall(r"Particle .*?rel\.err=([0-9.eE+\-]+)", fd_text)]
virial_match = re.search(r"Virial test:.*rel\.err=([0-9.eE+\-]+)", fd_text)
if len(force_errors) == 0 or virial_match is None:
    raise ValueError("Force or virial errors not found in the b3 force-test output")

max_force_error = max(force_errors)
virial_error = float(virial_match.group(1))

fd_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Test": ["Maximum particle force error", "Virial error"],
    "Relative error": [max_force_error, virial_error],
})
display(fd_table)

print()
print(f"Maximum force relative error = {max_force_error:.6e}")
print(f"Virial relative error        = {virial_error:.6e}")
print("Finite-difference displacement = 1e-6 Angstrom")
print(f"Accepted force tolerance       = {FD_TOL:g}")


# --- Noise floor of the finite-difference test ---------------------------
# Rounding in U is about eps*|U|. Dividing by the step delta gives an ABSOLUTE force error.
delta = 1e-6
eps_machine = np.finfo(float).eps
U_scale = abs(nve_1fs["Epot"].mean())
force_noise = 16.0 * eps_machine * U_scale / delta

print()
print(f"Estimated absolute finite-difference force resolution = {force_noise:.3e}")

# Analytical force vectors that were tested (one row per particle: fx, fy, fz)
force_vectors = np.array(
    re.findall(
        r"Particle\s+\d+:\s+Force analytical:\s*"
        r"\(\s*([0-9.eE+\-]+)\s*,\s*([0-9.eE+\-]+)\s*,\s*([0-9.eE+\-]+)\s*\)",
        fd_text,
    ),
    dtype=float,
)
magnitudes = np.linalg.norm(force_vectors, axis=1)
magnitudes = magnitudes[magnitudes > 0]          # ignore exactly zero forces, if any

min_force = magnitudes.min()
median_force = np.median(magnitudes)

# The floor is absolute, so it is worst for the smallest force
worst_floor = force_noise / min_force
typical_floor = force_noise / median_force

print()
print("Finite-difference tolerance estimate")
print("------------------------------------")
print(f"Smallest tested analytical force = {min_force:.6e}")
print(f"Median tested analytical force   = {median_force:.6e}")
print(f"Absolute FD noise estimate        = {force_noise:.6e}")
print(f"Worst estimated relative floor    = {worst_floor:.6e}")
print(f"Typical estimated relative floor  = {typical_floor:.6e}")
print(f"Observed maximum relative error   = {max_force_error:.6e}")
print(f"Chosen relative tolerance         = {FD_TOL:.6e}")

B5) Test the bonded forces¶

Finite-difference verification per bonded term, on a single molecule, plus long-time NVE energy conservation for that single molecule.

A freshly built chain sits exactly at the minimum of its bond, angle and torsion terms, so all three bonded forces are zero there and the check compares round-off with round-off: it reports large relative errors on perfectly correct code, and it would equally pass code that is wrong. B6) Initialization¶

Devise a procedure to pack N pentane molecules in a cubic box at the target density with a sane starting structure (reasonable internal geometry, and no overlap so severe that the first step throws a molecule across the box), and assign velocities from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at the target temperature.

Deliver: a description of your procedure, the box size and N you chose with the arithmetic that connects them to ρ=626 kg/m3, the closest interacting pair distance your configuration starts with next to σ, and a rendering of the starting configuration. Open it in OVITO and look at it, which is the point of the exercise; the figure in your report may come from OVITO, from VMD, or from your own plot of the .pdb, as long as it travels in the zip.

A lattice of chains is not a liquid, and a packing dense enough to hit the target density will have pairs inside σ. That is expected. B7 is where you measure what they cost.

B7) Energy conservation of the full system¶

From the packed configuration, run NVE and check energy conservation.

Deliver a figure of Etot, Ekin, Epot and T against time, and an explanation of the initial transient: the temperature moves within the first picoseconds even though the total energy does not. Where does that kinetic energy come from, and what does it tell you about your starting structure?

Answer B6-B7: Initialisation and full-system NVE¶

B6: Initialisation¶

System size

  • We use N=400 molecules, which gives 400×5=2000 sites.
  • Each molecule has two CH3 and three CH2 sites.

Box size from the density

Step Calculation Result
Mass of one molecule 2(15.035) + 3(14.027) 72.151 amu
Total mass 400 × 72.151 × 1.66054×10-27 4.7924×10-23 kg
Volume m/ρ = 4.7924×10-23 / 626 7.6556×10-26 m3
Box length L = V1/3 4.2461×10-9 m = 42.461 Å

Packing procedure

  • We put the 400 molecule centres on a 10×10×4 grid.
  • Each molecule is built all-trans, with r0=1.54 Å and θ0=114∘, so its internal geometry is sane.
  • We rotate the zig-zag plane of each molecule at random about its long axis.

Velocities

  • We draw them from a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at 293 K, using the right mass for each site type.
  • Then we remove the centre-of-mass momentum.

Closest interacting pair

Quantity Value
Closest pair CH2-CH2
Distance rmin 3.240 Å
σ for this pair 3.95 Å
rmin/σ 0.820
  • Why is this expected? The LJ energy is zero at r=σ and strongly repulsive below it. A packing dense enough to reach 626 kg/m3 always has some pairs inside σ.

Rendering

  • The box is filled and has no catastrophic overlaps.
  • The ordered arrangement is clearly not yet a liquid.

B7: NVE of the packed system¶

  • We ran with a 1 fs time step for about 20 ps, with the thermostat off. The figure is below.
Quantity Value
Relative drift (linear fit) -1.15×10-5 ps-1
Total systematic change over 20 ps about 0.023 %
Temperature after the transient about 200-205 K
  • Etot is approximately constant.

The initial transient

  • The temperature starts at 293 K, drops during the first few ps, and then fluctuates around 200-205 K. The total energy does not change.
  • Assigning velocities at 293 K only sets the initial kinetic energy. It does not make the configuration an equilibrium one.
  • Etot=Ekin+Epot is constant, so energy moves between the two.
  • In our run Epot rises and Ekin falls, so T falls.
  • Why does T fall? The temperature is proportional to the kinetic energy. The kinetic energy is not lost: it becomes potential energy.
  • What this says about our start: it is a reasonable starting point, but it is an artificial grid structure and not an equilibrated liquid.
In [4]:

B8) Thermostat¶

Implement the Berendsen thermostat for NVT runs.

B9) Test the thermostat¶

Starting from the packed configuration, run NVT and verify equilibration to the target temperature.

Deliver:

  • a figure of the temperature against time for NVE and for NVT, with two values of the coupling time τ, on one set of axes;
  • a table of the mean temperature and its fluctuation over the equilibrated part of each run, next to the target 293 K;
  • a comment on the trade-off: what does a very short τ buy you, and what does it cost? What is the Berendsen thermostat not guaranteed to give you, however well it holds the mean temperature?

Answer B8-B9: Thermostat and its test¶

B8: Berendsen thermostat¶

  • Where: thermostat() in dynamics.c.
  • Step 1: compute the current temperature from the kinetic energy:

T=2Ekin3N−3.

  • Step 2: multiply every velocity by the factor

λ=1+ΔtτT(T0T−1).

  • Why this form? We want the temperature to relax towards T0 with time constant τT, that is dT/dt=(T0−T)/τT. Kinetic energy, and so T, scales with λ2 when we scale velocities by λ. So one step needs λ2T=T+ΔtτT(T0−T). Dividing by T gives the formula.
  • Meaning:
    • If T<T0, then λ>1 and the system is heated.
    • If T>T0, then λ<1 and the system is cooled.

B9: Test¶

  • We ran three simulations from the same packed start:
    • NVE (the run from B7),
    • NVT with τ=0.01 ps,
    • NVT with τ=1.0 ps.
  • We computed the mean and the standard deviation of T over the last 5 ps (t≥15 ps), after the initial relaxation. The figure and the table are below.
Run Mean T (K) Std of T (K) Target (K)
NVE 204.07 2.61 293
NVT, τ = 0.01 ps 292.99 1.62 293
NVT, τ = 1.0 ps 291.67 3.52 293
  • NVE stays far below the target, consistent with B7.
  • Both NVT runs approach 293 K.

Trade-off of the coupling time¶

Short τ (0.01 ps) Long τ (1.0 ps)
Equilibration fast slow
Temperature fluctuation small (1.62 K) larger (3.52 K)
Disturbance of the dynamics strong, because velocities are rescaled aggressively weak

What Berendsen does not guarantee¶

  • It does not guarantee the correct canonical (NVT) ensemble.
  • The mean temperature can be right while the distribution and the size of the temperature and energy fluctuations are wrong.
  • Strong coupling suppresses the fluctuations artificially.
In [5]:

Part C: Production runs and analysis¶

In the oral you should be able to: predict how each observable moves when temperature, density or a force-field parameter changes; explain the pentane effect from the force field; defend where your MSD fit starts and your error estimate for D.

Part C is measurement, so every number needs an uncertainty and every figure needs axis labels with units, a legend, and a sentence stating what the reader should conclude.

Equilibrate before you sample, and check that you did. Both measurements below have their own relaxation time, and neither is short: the conformer populations relax over tens of picoseconds, and so does the sharing of kinetic energy between the chain ends and the chain interior after the starting lattice melts. Sampling from a configuration that is still relaxing biases the answer in a direction you can predict but will not see. Discard enough of the beginning of each production run that the quantity you are about to measure has stopped drifting, and say in your report how you decided how much was enough.

C1) Conformational analysis: the two dihedrals of pentane¶

Pentane has two coupled torsion angles (ϕ1,ϕ2). Classify each as trans (t, near 180∘) or gauche (g+ or g−, near ±60∘) and measure the populations of the pair states.

Deliver:

  • a figure: the joint distribution of (ϕ1,ϕ2) as a 2D histogram, with the state regions identifiable;
  • a figure: the one-dimensional distribution of a single dihedral, with the trans and gauche minima marked;
  • a table of the pair-state populations. Think about which states are equivalent by symmetry before you present nine numbers, and give each population an error estimate;
  • the pentane effect: compare g+g+ with g+g− explicitly. Explain the difference from the force field: which interaction penalises g+g−, and what happens geometrically to the two end groups in that conformation?
  • convergence: the barriers are several kBT, so transitions are rare events. Estimate, or measure from your trajectory, the mean time a molecule spends in a state, and use it to argue how long a run must be for the populations to be converged. Compare that with the length of the run you actually did, and say honestly whether your populations are converged.

Answer C1: Conformational analysis¶

Method¶

  • What we measured. During the production runs the code (analysis.c, called from main) computes both dihedrals of all 400 molecules every 0.1 ps, so we get 400 pairs (ϕ1,ϕ2) per sample.
  • Angle convention. IUPAC: ϕ=atan2 of the two plane normals, so trans is ±180∘ and g+ is +60∘. Its cosine is the cosϕ of A2 and of the torsion routine, which is why the minimum of Utors sits at 180∘.
  • State boundaries. trans: |ϕ|>120∘. g+: 0∘<ϕ<120∘. g−: −120∘<ϕ<0∘. The boundaries are at the tops of the barriers (see the free-energy figure), so a molecule that is in a well stays in its state.
  • Data. 5-site chains, 400 molecules, 4 independent replicas (new Maxwell-Boltzmann velocities, same equilibrated start). Each replica: 100 ps NVT equilibration (Berendsen, τ=1 ps), then 300 ps NVE production, of which the first 100 ps are discarded (see below). Data used: 200 ps per replica, 0.8 ns in total, 3.2 million (ϕ1,ϕ2) samples. Commands are in the Build & run log.
  • Equivalent states. Mirror symmetry and the symmetry between the two ends of the molecule leave only four distinct classes of the nine pair states:
Class States it contains Number
tt tt 1
tg tg+, tg-, g+t, g-t 4
g+g+ g+g+, g-g- 2
g+g- g+g-, g-g+ 2

How much to discard (equilibration)¶

Two quantities relax, and they relax on different time scales. Each replica starts from the melted state of B9 (20 ps old) with fresh velocities. We checked both.

  • Kinetic energy shared between chain ends and interior (first figure). We follow TCH3−TCH2, which is 0 in equilibrium. It is 13-15 K right after the restart, still 5.0 K at the end of the 100 ps equilibration, 3.4 K in the first 100 ps of production, and 1.3 K and 1.0 K in the next two 100 ps. So this relaxation is slower than the conformers, and 100 ps of NVT was not enough.
  • Conformer populations (second figure, 10 ps blocks of the equilibration). Comparing the first 50 ps with the last 50 ps: tt, tg and g+g+ differ by less than about one standard error. Only g+g− is still going down (by about 15 %, roughly 2 standard errors).
  • Decision: we discard the first 100 ps of each NVE production run, in addition to the 100 ps NVT equilibration and the 20 ps before it. After that, TCH3−TCH2 is about 1 K (0.3% of T) and no longer shows a trend. We chose 100 ps because the temperature difference has fallen to a few ×1 K by then; we cannot show it is exactly 0, because a replica's difference fluctuates by about 1-2 K. The conformer populations change by at most 0.005 when the first 100 ps are included (tt 0.468 instead of 0.473, about 2 standard errors), so this discard matters most for C2.

Results¶

Class Population s.e. (4 replicas) Per single state
tt 0.473 0.003 0.473
tg (4 states) 0.483 0.002 0.121
g+g+ + g-g- 0.0413 0.0013 0.0206
g+g- + g-g+ 0.00236 0.00013 0.00118
  • The standard error is the spread of the four replica values divided by 4. The 8 blocks of 100 ps (the used part of each replica) give errors of the same size (within a factor of 1.5, see the printed table).
  • The full 3×3 table is printed below the code. It is symmetric within the noise, as it should be. For example the two tg states with ϕ1=t are 0.122 and 0.124, and the g+g+ and g−g− entries are 0.0215 and 0.0198 (8 % apart, about 2 standard errors). We take the latter as a sign that the sampling noise of the rare classes is a bit larger than the s.e. from 4 replicas.
  • Figures. The joint histogram shows nine regions with the state boundaries; the four corners and the edges (tt, tg) are bright and the g+g− regions are almost empty. The 1D distribution has the trans maximum at ±180∘ and the gauche maxima at ±62.5∘ (probability maximum = potential minimum). The barrier top is near 117∘.
  • Free-energy check. −kBTlnP(ϕ) lies almost on top of the bare torsion potential. The gauche well is 476 K above trans (the torsion potential alone: 412 K), and the trans-to-gauche barrier is 1668 K =5.7kBT. So the single-dihedral distribution is essentially the Boltzmann factor of Utors; the extra interactions only show up in the pair statistics.

The pentane effect¶

  • Observation. Per state, g+g+ is 17.5 times more probable than g+g− (replicas: 22, 18, 17, 14). If the two dihedrals were independent, both would be P(g+)2 and the ratio would be 1. The cost of g+g− relative to g+g+ is −kBTln(0.00118/0.0206)=838 K =2.9kBT.
  • Which interaction. The Lennard-Jones interaction between the two end groups, the 1-5 pair. It is the first pair in the chain that is not excluded (1-2, 1-3 and 1-4 are), so it is the only term that couples ϕ1 and ϕ2 beyond the two torsion potentials.
  • Geometry. We built the ideal chain (r0=1.54 Å, θ0=114∘) and measured the 1-5 distance:
Conformer 1-5 distance (Å) relative to σ33=3.75 Å
tt 5.17 1.38
tg 4.56 1.21
g+g+ 3.76 1.00
g+g- 2.87 0.76
  • In g+g+ the chain curls like a helix and the end groups sit about one σ apart: no net LJ energy (about −8 K). In g+g− the second turn goes the opposite way, the chain folds back on itself, and the end groups are pushed to 0.76 σ, where the CH3-CH3 repulsion is ~8×103 K at the ideal geometry. The molecule cannot afford that, so it opens its angles and twists the dihedrals away from ±60∘ (see the smeared g+g− blobs in the histogram) and pays 838 K instead. This is the syn-pentane interaction.
  • Prediction. If the 1-5 pair did not interact (set ϵ33=0 for that pair), g+g+ and g+g− would be equally likely. We did not run that test.

Convergence¶

  • Residence times (from the counted transitions at 0.1 ps resolution, pooled over replicas): a dihedral stays 36 ps in trans and 15 ps in gauche. The relaxation time of the two-state process is 1/(ktg+kgt)=10.4 ps.
  • Estimate of the needed run length. The barrier is 5.7kBT, so a transition has probability about e−5.7 per attempt, which explains tens of ps. To measure a population to a few % you need the dihedral to have visited each state many times, so many relaxation times. For one molecule we use 200 ps =19 relaxation times, so a single molecule's populations are only roughly converged: its trace (third figure) shows long stays and a few jumps.
  • What we actually have. 4×200 ps × 800 dihedrals ≈61,000 relaxation times in total, if all dihedrals were independent. That is optimistic, because the two dihedrals of a molecule are coupled and all replicas start from the same configuration, but the molecules are in a liquid and decorrelate from each other quickly.
  • Verdict.
    • tt, tg and g+g+: converged to better than 1 %-3 % (replica s.e. ≤0.003; the binomial estimate with Neff is within a factor of 2 of it).
    • g+g−: statistically fine (5 % s.e.), but we do not fully trust it. It is the one conformer class still drifting at the end of the equilibration, and its binomial error with Neff (8 %) is larger than the replica spread, which suggests the replica s.e. is too small. We quote it as 0.0024±0.0002 and would say ±10% in the oral.
    • The conclusion that g+g+≫g+g− does not depend on any of this: the ratio is above 14 in each replica.

Likely oral questions¶

  • Why do you merge states? Mirror image molecules have equal energy, and the molecule has no preferred end, so those states are exactly equivalent. Merging them gives better statistics, and the symmetry of the 3×3 table is a check on the sampling.
  • Why not look at the single-dihedral distribution only? It is just the Boltzmann factor of Utors (the two curves coincide). The pentane effect is a statement about the pair.
  • Why do you need an equilibration run? The starting configuration is a melted lattice. Its conformer populations are those of the lattice, not of the liquid.
  • Is 0.0024 reliable? It is an estimate to about 10 %; see the convergence discussion.
In [6]:

N_BINS = 72
BIN_DEG = 360 / N_BINS
CENTRES = -180 + BIN_DEG * (np.arange(N_BINS) + 0.5)       # bin centres in degrees
STATE_OF_BIN = np.where(np.abs(CENTRES) > 120, 0, np.where(CENTRES > 0, 1, 2))
STATE_NAMES = ["t", "g+", "g-"]                              # trans |phi| > 120, g+ 0..120, g- -120..0


def joint_matrix(hist):
    """3x3 matrix of counts: rows = state of phi1, columns = state of phi2."""
    m = np.zeros((3, 3))
    np.add.at(m, (STATE_OF_BIN[hist["bin1"].to_numpy()], STATE_OF_BIN[hist["bin2"].to_numpy()]),
              hist["count"].to_numpy())
    return m


def classes(m):
    """Symmetry-reduced populations (fractions): tt, tg, g+g+, g+g-."""
    m = m / m.sum()
    return np.array([
        m[0, 0],                                  # tt
        m[0, 1] + m[0, 2] + m[1, 0] + m[2, 0],    # tg+, tg-, g+t, g-t
        m[1, 1] + m[2, 2],                        # g+g+, g-g-
        m[1, 2] + m[2, 1],                        # g+g-, g-g+
    ])


CLASS_NAMES = ["tt", "tg (4 states)", "g+g+ and g-g- (2)", "g+g- and g-g+ (2)"]
N_EQUIV = np.array([1, 4, 2, 2])

# --- Equilibration check 1: do the chain ends and the interior share kinetic energy? ------
# After the lattice melts the CH3 ends are hotter than the CH2 interior; T_CH3 - T_CH2 must go to 0.
BLOCK_PS = 100.0
DISCARD_PS = 100.0                                      # first part of each production run that is thrown away
FIRST_BLOCK = int(round(DISCARD_PS / BLOCK_PS))          # production blocks of 100 ps: blocks below this are discarded


def type_temperature_difference(thermo, offset_ps, bin_ps=10.0):
    time_ps = thermo["time"].to_numpy(float) * PS_PER_TIME_UNIT + offset_ps
    diff = (thermo["T_CH3_K"] - thermo["T_CH2_K"]).to_numpy(float)
    bins = np.floor(time_ps / bin_ps).astype(int)
    return (np.array([time_ps[bins == b].mean() for b in np.unique(bins)]),
            np.array([diff[bins == b].mean() for b in np.unique(bins)]))

    t_e, d_e = type_temperature_difference(equil_thermo[k], 0.0)
    t_p, d_p = type_temperature_difference(prod_thermo[k], equil_end)
    ax.plot(np.r_[t_e, t_p], np.r_[d_e, d_p], lw=1, alpha=0.8, label=f"replica {k + 1}")
    curves.append((t_p - equil_end, d_p))

C2) Diffusion coefficient¶

Implement creation and on-the-fly updating of the mean squared displacement of the molecular centres of mass, and extract the self-diffusion coefficient D from the long-time slope, ⟨Δr2⟩→6Dt.

Deliver:

  • a figure of the MSD against time on log-log axes, with the ballistic (∝t2) and diffusive (∝t) regimes marked, and the fit window shown;
  • the value of D in internal units and in m2/s, with an error estimate and a statement of how you obtained it (for example by splitting the trajectory into blocks and comparing);
  • a sentence justifying where your fit window starts and ends: why not earlier, why not later?

Then compare your D with an experimental value for liquid pentane if you can find one, and say what a disagreement would mean: an error in your code, or a limitation of the model?

Answer C2: Diffusion coefficient¶

Implementation¶

  • Where: analysis.c (analysis_update, sample_msd), called every step from main.
  • Unwrapped positions. The code wraps positions into the box every step, which would make the MSD saturate at the box size. We therefore add the per-step displacement dr (already stored by update_positions) to a second array r_unwrapped. It is never wrapped.
  • Molecular centres of mass. For each molecule the mass-weighted mean of its five unwrapped sites. This removes the fast internal vibrations, which are not diffusion.
  • MSD with many time origins. Every 1 ps a new origin is stored (the last 100 are kept); every 10 fs the squared displacement from each stored origin is averaged over the 400 molecules and added to the bin of that lag. That gives up to 300 origins per lag and a maximum lag of 100 ps.
  • Runs: the same 4 NVE production replicas as in C1 (4 × 300 ps). NVE is used because the thermostat would rescale velocities, and with it the dynamics.
  • What is discarded: the time origins of the first 100 ps of each production run. They are in block 0 of the MSD file; the MSD used is the average of the blocks of origins from 100-200 ps and 200-300 ps. The reason is the slow sharing of kinetic energy between chain ends and interior (see C1): the ends are still hotter by about 3 K during the first 100 ps. The printout shows that the origins from the first 100 ps give a 5 % larger D (7.06×10−9 against 6.68 and 6.93×10−9 m2/s for the next two blocks, each with a standard error of about 0.1×10−9).
  • Sanity checks of the runs (printed below the code): mean temperature 292.5-293.5 K, relative drift of Etot below 4×10−7 per ps, so the dynamics are a clean NVE trajectory at the target temperature. After the discarded 100 ps, TCH3−TCH2 is 0.4-2.2 K in the four replicas.

Results¶

Quantity Value
Fit window 10 - 50 ps (MSD linear in t)
D (internal units) 0.747 ± 0.008 Å2 per internal time unit
D (SI) (6.81 ± 0.07)×10-9 m2/s
Finite-size correction +0.60×10-9 m2/s (+9 %)
D∞ ≈ 7.4×10-9 m2/s
  • How we got the error. We fit the slope of each replica's MSD in the window, D=slope/6, and quote the standard deviation of the four values divided by 4. The four replicas give D={0.679,0.693,0.662,0.689} \AA2/ps. The error is statistical only.
  • Unit conversion. 1 \AA2/ps=10−8 m2/s, and 1 internal time unit =1.0967 ps, so Dinternal=1.0967D\AA2/ps.
  • Sensitivity to the window. Moving the window (5-30, 10-30, 10-80, 20-60, 20-90 ps) changes D between 6.80 and 6.88×10−9 m2/s, which is within about one standard error (the longer windows have larger errors). So the window choice is not an important error source.

The figure¶

  • At short times the MSD follows the ballistic line ⟨Δr2⟩=(3kBT/M)t2, which we draw without any fit (molecule mass M=72.151 amu). The measured MSD at 0.1 ps is 0.096 \AA2 against 0.101 from this line (5 % lower, as expected at 0.1 ps, where the molecule has already started to collide).
  • The local slope falls from 2 to about 1 between 0.1 and 2 ps (the molecule collides with its neighbours) and stays at 1 afterwards: the diffusive regime.

Fit window: why there¶

  • Why not earlier. Before about 2 ps the slope is above 1.1: the MSD is still bending from ballistic to diffusive, and a straight line would be biased. We start at 10 ps to be safely in the linear regime. A free intercept b also absorbs the remaining offset (the fit gives b=0.86 \AA2, small against MSD values of 40-300 \AA2 in the window).
  • Why not later. At large lags fewer time origins contribute (150 per replica at 50 ps, about 110 at 90 ps, because we dropped the first 100 ps) and they overlap heavily, so the noise grows (visible as the wiggles in the local slope above 50 ps). The window ends at 50 ps, half the maximum lag. Also, a lag of 50 ps corresponds to a root-mean-square displacement of 14 Å, one third of the box.

Comparison with experiment and what a disagreement would mean¶

  • Experimental value. About 5.6×10−9 m2/s for liquid n-pentane at 298 K. We found this value in a web search of a simulation-versus-experiment comparison; we have not checked it against the primary experimental paper, so treat it as approximate.
  • Our result. 6.8×10−9 (uncorrected) is 22 % above it; 7.4×10−9 after the finite-size correction is 32 % above. Our temperature (293 K) is 5 K lower than the experimental one, which would make our D smaller if anything, so the temperature does not explain it.
  • Finite-size correction. In a periodic box the hydrodynamic backflow slows diffusion by 2.837kBT/(6πηL) (Yeh-Hummer). We use η=0.24 mPa s (approximate literature viscosity) and L=42.46 Å. The correction is 9 % of D, so our simulated value is a lower bound of the bulk value for this model.
  • Interpretation. A 20-30 % difference is a limitation of the model, not a code error:
    • The united-atom model has no hydrogens, so the molecular surface is smoother than the real one and molecules slide past each other more easily. Such models are known to diffuse too fast.
    • The force field was fitted to thermodynamic data (density, vapour pressure), not to transport.
    • A bug in the MSD would show up as a wrong ballistic limit or a wrong slope, and neither does: the t2 line matches without fitting and the slope is 1.
    • A bug in the forces or the integrator is excluded by B3-B5 and B7 (energy conservation, finite-difference tests).
  • What would indicate a code error: a factor of order 2 or more, a diffusive slope different from 1, or D depending on the number of time origins.

Likely oral questions¶

  • Why molecular centres of mass and not single atoms? Atoms also vibrate and rotate within the molecule; the atomic MSD has the same long-time slope but a larger offset. The task asks for the centre of mass.
  • Why do we need unwrapped coordinates? Wrapping makes the MSD saturate at about L2/4.
  • Why 6? In 3D ⟨Δr2⟩=6Dt (Einstein, 2D per dimension).
  • Why NVE? The Berendsen thermostat rescales velocities and so alters the dynamics.

# C2: MSD vs time (log-log), fit window, D extraction with error estimate

# --- Load the MSD of each production replica -----------------------------
msd_runs = [
    load_csv("data/c_prod_1_msd.csv"),
    load_csv("data/c_prod_2_msd.csv"),
    load_csv("data/c_prod_3_msd.csv"),
    load_csv("data/c_prod_4_msd.csv"),
]
prod_runs = [
    load_csv("data/c_prod_1.csv"),
    load_csv("data/c_prod_2.csv"),
    load_csv("data/c_prod_3.csv"),
    load_csv("data/c_prod_4.csv"),
]

lag = msd_runs[0]["lag_ps"].to_numpy()
DISCARD_PS = 100.0                                                       # first part of each production run that is thrown away
# The MSD file holds one column per 100 ps block of time origins. The origins of block 0 start in the
# first 100 ps of production and are discarded; blocks 1 and 2 are averaged (equal weights).
msd_blocks = np.array([[run[f"block{b}"].to_numpy() for b in range(3)] for run in msd_runs])    # (replica, block, lag)
msd_rep = np.nanmean(msd_blocks[:, 1:, :], axis=1)                                             # (replica, lag), A^2
msd = msd_rep.mean(axis=0)
msd_sem = msd_rep.std(axis=0, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(msd_rep))

# --- Sanity check of the production runs: NVE energy and temperature -----
for k, run in enumerate(prod_runs, start=1):
    drift = energy_drift(run["time"].to_numpy(float) * PS_PER_TIME_UNIT, run["Etot"].to_numpy(float))
    print(f"Replica {k}: mean T = {run['T'].mean():.2f} K (std {run['T'].std():.2f}), "
          f"relative E_tot drift = {drift['rel_drift']:.2e} per ps, relative oscillation = {drift['rel_oscillation']:.2e}")

for k, run in enumerate(prod_runs, start=1):
    late = run["time"] * PS_PER_TIME_UNIT >= DISCARD_PS
    print(f"Replica {k}, after the first {DISCARD_PS:.0f} ps: T = {run.loc[late, 'T'].mean():.2f} K, "
          f"T_CH3 - T_CH2 = {(run.loc[late, 'T_CH3_K'] - run.loc[late, 'T_CH2_K']).mean():.2f} K")

# --- Ballistic regime: <dR^2> = 3 k_B T / M_mol * t^2 (no fit) ------------
M_MOL = 2 * 15.035 + 3 * 14.027                                  # amu = internal mass units
msd_ballistic = (3 * T_TARGET / M_MOL) * (lag / PS_PER_TIME_UNIT) ** 2

# --- Local slope d ln(MSD) / d ln(t): 2 = ballistic, 1 = diffusive --------
positive = lag > 0
log_t = np.log(lag[positive])
local_slope = np.gradient(np.log(msd[positive]), log_t)

# --- Linear fit MSD = 6 D t + b in a window -------------------------------
FIT_START_PS = 10.0
FIT_END_PS = 50.0
window = (lag >= FIT_START_PS) & (lag <= FIT_END_PS)


def fit_D(msd_curve):
    """Slope of MSD against t in the window, converted to D (A^2 per ps)."""
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(lag[window], msd_curve[window], 1)
    return slope / 6.0, intercept


D_each = np.array([fit_D(m)[0] for m in msd_rep])                # A^2 / ps, one per replica
D_total, intercept_total = fit_D(msd)
D_mean = D_each.mean()
D_sem = D_each.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(D_each))

A2_PER_PS_TO_M2_PER_S = 1e-20 / 1e-12                            # 1 A^2/ps = 1e-8 m^2/s
D_internal = D_mean * PS_PER_TIME_UNIT                           # A^2 per internal time unit
D_internal_sem = D_sem * PS_PER_TIME_UNIT
D_si = D_mean * A2_PER_PS_TO_M2_PER_S
D_si_sem = D_sem * A2_PER_PS_TO_M2_PER_S

print()
print(f"Fit window: {FIT_START_PS:.0f} - {FIT_END_PS:.0f} ps")
print(f"D per replica (A^2/ps) = {np.round(D_each, 5)}")
print(f"D = {D_internal:.4f} +- {D_internal_sem:.4f} A^2 per internal time unit (internal units)")
print(f"D = {D_si:.3e} +- {D_si_sem:.1e} m^2/s   (mean +- standard error over 4 replicas)")
print(f"Fit of the replica-averaged MSD gives D = {D_total * A2_PER_PS_TO_M2_PER_S:.3e} m^2/s, intercept b = {intercept_total:.2f} A^2")

# --- Why the first 100 ps are discarded: D from each block of time origins --------------
block_D = np.array([[np.polyfit(lag[window], b[window], 1)[0] / 6.0 for b in rep_blocks] for rep_blocks in msd_blocks]) * A2_PER_PS_TO_M2_PER_S
print()
print("D (m^2/s) from the time origins of each 100 ps block of the production run (mean over replicas +- s.e.)")
for b in range(3):
    print(f"  origins from {100 * b:3d}-{100 * (b + 1):3d} ps: D = {block_D[:, b].mean():.3e} +- {block_D[:, b].std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(block_D)):.1e}")

# --- Sensitivity of D to the window -------------------------------------
rows = []
for start, end in [(5, 30), (10, 30), (10, 50), (10, 80), (20, 60), (20, 90)]:
    sel = (lag >= start) & (lag <= end)
    d_rep = np.array([np.polyfit(lag[sel], m[sel], 1)[0] / 6.0 for m in msd_rep]) * A2_PER_PS_TO_M2_PER_S
    rows.append({"Window (ps)": f"{start}-{end}", "D (m^2/s)": d_rep.mean(), "s.e. (m^2/s)": d_rep.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(d_rep))})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows))

# --- Finite-size correction (Yeh-Hummer) and comparison with experiment ---
KB = 1.380649e-23
L_BOX = 42.4612104e-10                                           # m
ETA_PENTANE = 0.24e-3                                            # Pa s, liquid n-pentane near 293 K (literature value, approximate)
D_correction = 2.837 * KB * T_TARGET / (6 * np.pi * ETA_PENTANE * L_BOX)
D_experiment = 5.6e-9                                            # m^2/s at 298 K, see the answer text for the source
print()
print(f"Finite-size correction 2.837 k_B T / (6 pi eta L) = {D_correction:.2e} m^2/s ({100 * D_correction / D_si:.0f} % of D)")
print(f"D corrected to infinite system = {D_si + D_correction:.3e} m^2/s")
print(f"Experimental D (298 K) = {D_experiment:.2e} m^2/s -> simulation / experiment = {D_si / D_experiment:.2f} "
      f"(corrected: {(D_si + D_correction) / D_experiment:.2f})")

# --- Figure: MSD on log-log axes -----------------------------------------
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [2, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
ax.loglog(lag[positive], msd[positive], color="C0", lw=2, label=r"MSD of molecular centres of mass (mean of 4 replicas)")
ax.fill_between(lag[positive], (msd - msd_sem)[positive], (msd + msd_sem)[positive], color="C0", alpha=0.25)
ax.loglog(lag[positive], msd_ballistic[positive], "k--", label=r"ballistic, $3k_BT\,t^2/M$ (no fit)")
ax.loglog(lag[positive], (6 * D_mean * lag + intercept_total)[positive], "C3--", label=r"diffusive, $6Dt + b$ from the fit")
ax.axvspan(FIT_START_PS, FIT_END_PS, color="C2", alpha=0.2, label=f"fit window {FIT_START_PS:.0f}-{FIT_END_PS:.0f} ps")
ax.set_xlim(lag[positive].min(), lag.max())
ax.set_ylim(msd[positive].min(), msd.max() * 2)
ax.text(0.02, 0.08, r"slope 2 ($\propto t^2$)", transform=ax.transAxes, rotation=50)
ax.text(0.66, 0.78, r"slope 1 ($\propto t$)", transform=ax.transAxes, rotation=28)
ax.set_xlabel("Lag time (ps)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\langle |\Delta \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{cm}|^2 \rangle$ ($\mathrm{\AA}^2$)")
ax.set_title("Mean-squared displacement of n-pentane at 293 K")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")

ax = axes[1]
ax.semilogx(lag[positive], local_slope, color="C0")
ax.axhline(1, color="C3", ls="--")
ax.axhline(2, color="k", ls="--")
ax.axvspan(FIT_START_PS, FIT_END_PS, color="C2", alpha=0.2)
ax.set_xlabel("Lag time (ps)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"local slope $d\ln \mathrm{MSD} / d\ln t$")
ax.set_ylim(0.5, 2.2)
ax.set_title("Where does the MSD become diffusive?")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Local slope reaches 1.1 at t = {lag[positive][np.argmax((local_slope < 1.1) & (lag[positive] > 0.5))]:.1f} ps; "
      f"time origins per replica at {FIT_END_PS:.0f} ps lag = {int(np.clip(300 - FIT_END_PS - DISCARD_PS, 0, 200))} (1 ps apart, from 100 ps to 300 ps minus the lag)")

Lessons learned¶

What would you do differently if you started over? What surprised you? What in your results still bothers you? (Standing questions in the oral, so write the honest version.)

Lessons learned: (draft by Claude from what happened; edit before the oral)

  • What we would do differently.
    • Record every run (command, parameters, AI tools used) when it is made. For B1-B9 we had to write "not recorded", and for B4-B9 we still do not know which AI tools were used.
    • Equilibrate the packed start properly (a long NVT run) before B7-B9. The 200 K temperature in B7 is the signature of a lattice that has not melted, and every later run had to start from it.
    • Equilibrate the C runs longer, and monitor the CH3-CH2 temperature difference from the start: 100 ps of NVT was not enough, and we had to discard the first 100 ps of production.
    • Plan C as replicas from the start. Running 4 short independent runs gave an honest error bar and used the cores of the machine.
  • What surprised us.
    • The single-dihedral distribution is exactly the Boltzmann factor of the torsion potential, and the whole pentane effect hides in the pair statistics: g+g+ is 18 times more likely than g+g−.
    • The MSD is diffusive from about 2 ps already, much earlier than we expected, so the fit window is not critical.
  • What still bothers us.
    • D is 22-32 % above the experimental value. We argue this is the united-atom model (and the finite box makes it even larger after correction), but we did not test it, for example with a different force field or temperature.
    • We found the experimental D by a web search and did not verify it against the original paper.
    • The rare g+g− class was still drifting during the equilibration; our error on it is probably too optimistic.
    • The g+g+ and g−g− populations differ by 8 % although they must be equal by symmetry: the error from four replicas underestimates the sampling noise of the rare classes.
    • We did not run the control that switches the 1-5 interaction off, so we only argue from geometry that the end-group LJ term causes the pentane effect.

Hand-in¶

One zip per group, layout exactly:

<group>_A2.zip
├── A2.ipynb     this notebook, filled in and executed
│                (all outputs present; task cells untouched)
├── A2.html      python3 nb2html.py A2.ipynb
├── code/        all .c/.h + README.md; must build with
│                gcc -O3 *.c -o md -lm    (no binaries)
└── data/        every data file this notebook loads

Long production runs are done in the terminal; record the exact commands in the Build & run log and let the notebook load the saved output from data/. Handed in executed, the notebook must open and display without rerunning anything.

Write the path of every data file your notebook opens out in full, as "data/run.csv" rather than assembling it from a variable. The checker below looks for those paths literally, and it will report a file as missing if it cannot see the name.

Before you submit, check your own zip:

python3 check_my_submission.py <group>_A2.zip --release A2.ipynb

where --release is a freshly downloaded, unmodified A2.ipynb. It verifies the layout, that the task cells are untouched, that every cell has been executed, that your C code compiles, and that every path and link in the notebook is relative and present in the zip. Fix what it reports, then submit. Setting up the Python environment (requirements.txt, both helper scripts) is described on the Canvas page Working on the assignments.
